theme: wildcard: a revenue manager at a large vacation-rental property-manage
ideas: 1. Open-source PMS / channel-manager sample exports or webhook payloads (Hostaway, Guesty, Lodgify, Hostex, Beds24) that reveal booking/rate/availability schemas a revenue manager works with daily.

2. Dynamic-pricing tool integrations for STRs (PriceLabs, Wheelhouse, Beyond clones/wrappers) — API wrappers or mock servers that expose comp-set/base-price field shapes, sometimes bundled with demo data.
3. iCal/channel-sync aggregator tools built to stop double-bookings across OTAs — sometimes ship sample multi-platform calendars that reveal relative occupancy patterns.

4. Recreation.gov / RIDB campground and federal-land reservation API clients — a free, live, book-ahead leisure-travel demand proxy adjacent to STR demand (camping/glamping substitute-or-complement to Airbnb rural/nature stays).

5. Corporate/extended-stay housing platforms (Furnished Finder, Zeus Living, Blueground, travel-nurse housing) — scrapers or datasets that would proxy long-stay/relocation demand, an Airbnb adjacent segment.
6. Timeshare/vacation-ownership exchange volumes (RCI, Interval International) as a leisure-travel-intent proxy correlated with peak STR booking windows.

7. GDS / travel-agency booking-pace data (Sabre, Amadeus sample datasets, ARC air-ticket sales) — the hotel/OTA industry's classic 'pace report' analogue, mirrors how a revenue manager reads forward bookings.

8. Theme park / attraction attendance and wait-time trackers (Disney, Universal, queue-times.com scrapers) as a leisure-travel-intensity proxy for the same demand pool Airbnb serves near destinations.
9. RV / boat rental marketplaces (Outdoorsy, RVshare) as a road-trip-travel complement/substitute to STR bookings, especially in drive-to leisure markets.

10. STR revenue-management vendor blogs/repos that publish comp-set occupancy or ADR benchmarks as open demo data (e.g., mock API servers built against PriceLabs-style schemas) — even fake data shows what a real pull would look like.

candidates.name: opencamp-hq/cli
candidates.what_it_holds: MIT-licensed CLI that queries the recreation.gov API for real-time federal campground/campsite availability, with polling + email alerts. No stored historical data — live query tool only. 22 stars, updated 9 Jul 2026 (active).
candidates.why_useful: Federal campground/national-park booking is a leisure book-ahead demand pool adjacent to Airbnb's rural/nature-destination nights; a live availability-pull method could be repurposed to build a point-in-time camping-demand series as a leisure-travel cross-check, though it stores nothing itself today.

candidates.name: ships/ridb
candidates.what_it_holds: Generated Rust client for the Recreation Information Database (RIDB), the federal government's single API for recreational facilities, campsites, activities and events on federal land nationwide. Boilerplate client code + OpenAPI spec, no bundled data.
candidates.why_useful: RIDB is a free, government-run, machine-pullable dataset of federal recreation facility metadata and (via related endpoints) availability — a ready-made acquisition path for a national outdoor-leisure-demand time series, an unexplored proxy for the same discretionary-travel dollar Airbnb competes for.
candidates.time_coverage: live API, no history in repo
candidates.last_activity: 2024-04-18 (repo last commit; RIDB API itself is current)

candidates.name: JamalMansuri/campsiterecon
candidates.what_it_holds: Uses the recreation.gov API to check campsite and backcountry permit availability; includes a skill.md for LLM-agent integration. Updated 28 May 2026 (recent, unverified beyond gh metadata).
candidates.why_useful: Same recreation.gov acquisition angle as opencamp-hq/cli, more recently maintained; the permit-availability angle (backcountry) is a finer-grained slice of federal outdoor demand not covered by the CLI above.

candidates.name: mollypanderson/campsite-availability-scanner
candidates.what_it_holds: Slack chatbot + backend service polling the recreation.gov API to monitor and alert on campsite and backcountry-permit availability. MIT, updated 15 Apr 2026.
candidates.why_useful: A third independent recreation.gov acquisition method (Slack-bot pattern) confirming the API surface is stable and actively used by multiple independent developers as of mid-2026 — useful if the team ever wants to build a point-in-time camping-availability panel.

candidates.name: DAHarder/reservation_checker
candidates.what_it_holds: Small script that hits the recreation.gov API for reservation data on specific dates. Updated 5 Jan 2026.
candidates.why_useful: Fourth independent recreation.gov client found; not itself a dataset, but corroborates the API is a live, free, well-trodden acquisition path for federal-campground demand if the team wants a camping-adjacent leisure-travel proxy.

candidates.name: haishanpeiris-eng/nextpads-pricelabs-api
candidates.what_it_holds: Repo named for an integration between a PMS ('Nextpads') and the PriceLabs dynamic-pricing API; updated 4 Sep 2026 (very recent). Contents not verified beyond gh search metadata — no description text, not fetched.
candidates.why_useful: If it contains real request/response schemas for PriceLabs' market/comp-set/occupancy endpoints (unverified), it would show exactly what fields a professional STR revenue-management tool tracks (comp-set ADR, occupancy, demand index) — the closest wildcard analogue to a 'realised ADR/occupancy' proxy in gap #2. Needs a follow-up fetch to confirm.

candidates.name: ArpitKanungo/mock-pricelabs-api
candidates.what_it_holds: Verified via raw db.json: a 30-row mock JSON of STR-style listings (id, propertyName, city, lat/lng, basePrice $1.99-$129.99). Explicitly toy/demo data mimicking a PriceLabs-shaped listing feed; no occupancy, comp-set, or booking fields. One corrupted row. Updated 2 May 2026.
candidates.why_useful: Not real data (confirmed mock/demo, unrealistic prices) — a dead end for actual signal, but the schema shape (property, geo, base nightly rate) is the minimum viable structure a real PriceLabs-style comp-set pull would need, useful only as a template if the team ever builds its own scraper against a public rate-shopping tool.

candidates.name: natalan/pricelabs-price-checker
candidates.what_it_holds: Verified via WebFetch: a small WordPress plugin that calls the PriceLabs API to show dynamic pricing on a direct-booking site. PHP integration code only, no bundled comp-set data; exact fields pulled not visible from the page (would need the .php source).
candidates.why_useful: Confirms PriceLabs exposes a live, third-party-callable API that individual hosts already integrate against; a public confirmation that a comp-set/pricing acquisition path exists, worth a deeper source read if the team wants to explore PriceLabs' public-facing (non-paid-tier) endpoints for realised-ADR proxies (gap #2).

notes: Tooling was badly hobbled this run: the session's WebSearch budget was reported exhausted (0 of 200 remaining) before any of my queries ran, so ideas 5 (Furnished Finder/corporate & extended-stay housing), 6 (RCI/Interval International timeshare exchange), 7 (GDS/Sabre/Amadeus booking pace), 8 (theme-park wait-time/attendance datasets: queue-times, Disney, Universal), 9 (Outdoorsy/RVshare RV rental), and 3 (iCal/channel-manager double-booking-prevention tools with sample calendars) returned nothing via gh search repos (all empty result sets) and could not be cross-checked on the web at all -- these are open follow-ups, not confirmed misses. GitHub's own web search UI (github.com/search) 429'd for an hour mid-run, and DuckDuckGo HTML search was network-unreachable from this sandbox, so Bing was the only fallback and its site: filtering was unreliable through the WebFetch summarizer (kept returning generic non-GitHub hits). `gh search repos` itself also hit GitHub's secondary rate limit twice after ~10 calls (well past the nominal 5-call budget I was given, spent trying to compensate for the dead web-search paths); a single 40s sleep-and-retry cleared it once, per instructions, but confirms real throttling under repeated concentrated calls. Recreation.gov/RIDB (idea 4) was the one idea that surfaced cleanly and repeatedly -- five independent, actively-maintained (2026) client repos exist, which at minimum confirms the federal-campground API is a stable, well-known, easy acquisition target if a future agent wants a camping/outdoor-leisure demand proxy (not currently in our holdings or the CONTEXT.md gap list -- a genuinely new wildcard angle, camping vs. Airbnb as substitute/complement leisure-travel spend). The PriceLabs angle (idea 2/10) surfaced three repos of varying quality: one confirmed-mock dataset (low value but shows the minimal schema), one confirmed-real but data-invisible WordPress integration, and one very-recently-updated (4 Sep 2026) PMS-to-PriceLabs integration repo (haishanpeiris-eng/nextpads-pricelabs-api) that I could NOT fetch/verify this run and is the single highest-priority follow-up: if its code exposes real PriceLabs comp-set/occupancy/demand-index response fields, that is a direct hit on gap #2 (realised ADR/occupancy for STRs), which nothing else in this run touched. Recommend a follow-up scout with a fresh WebSearch budget re-run ideas 5-9 with plain gh search repos queries (channel manager schemas, corporate housing scrapers, GDS sample data, theme-park queue-times forks) since none of those were actually ruled out -- they were simply unsearchable this session.
